paper_title: WorldFoundry: Towards Unified Infrastructure for World Intelligence

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Visual generative models increasingly blur the line between synthesizing observations and simulating environments. Yet visual plausibility alone does not constitute successful world modeling: compelling outputs may lack persistent state, physical dynamics, or causally consistent responses to interactions. We define a generative world model as a predictive dynamical system that maintains a persistent, history-conditioned representation of an environment, updates that representation in response to actions or interventions, and generates temporally coherent trajectories that reflect outcomes under observed and counterfactual interventions. From this definition, we derive an intelligence-oriented framework spanning perceptual grounding, persistent state modeling, controllable transformation, dynamics-aware prediction, and closed-loop interaction. We present WorldFoundry, open-source infrastructure for reproducible inference and evaluation across video, 3D and 4D, embodied action, and interactive world systems. WorldFoundry unifies model and benchmark discovery, runtime and asset preparation, execution orchestration, artifact management, and interactive visualization, while modality-specific adapters preserve native inputs, execution semantics, output representations, and evaluation protocols. Explicit manifests, durable artifact contracts, and evidence-aware scorecards separate execution readiness from evaluative claims, making each claim traceable to its supporting artifacts. The catalog contains 270 model entries, 74 benchmarks, and 62 registered metric entries, with readiness and execution evidence recorded separately. WorldFoundry enables reproducible comparison of persistent, controllable dynamics across heterogeneous systems, advancing the field from perceptual synthesis toward measurable world intelligence.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Figure 1 Overview of WorldFoundry. Open-source infrastructure for generative world models. (1) one run is reachable from every interactive and programmatic surface; (2) preflight requests execute through unified runner, one-shot or session-resident; (3) outputs are persisted behind durable artifact contracts with typed references; (4) benchmarks score persist in artifacts reported in an evidence scorecard; and (5) declarative manifests bind discovery, runtime and evaluation, keeping claims traceable to evidence. Recent advances in generative modeling are moving beyond synthesizing individual objects or scenes toward modeling worlds that evolve over time and respond to interventions. This shift calls for broader notion of world intelligence, in which systems must perceive observations, infer structured states, predict their evolution, express resulting consequences through task-specific outputs, and exploit these predictions for interaction [1 4]. Video generators, neural scene representations, and embodied policies address complementary parts of this problem. However, incompatible representations, runtimes, interfaces, and evaluation protocols make capabilities difficult to compose, results difficult to reproduce, and progress toward genuine world models difficult to measure. The bottleneck is therefore not only algorithmic, but also infrastructural. Recent efforts such as OpenWorldLib [5] address complementary aspects of this integration problem. Progress therefore requires shared infrastructure grounded in common functional abstraction that makes heterogeneous models composable, reproducible, and comparable across modalities while preserving their native semantics. To establish common ground without constraining how different systems represent the world, we formulate the abstraction at the level of function. Building on insights from earlier definitions in reinforcement learning [13] and recent efforts to delineate their scope [5], we identify three tightly coupled components. State inference estimates latent environmental state from the observation history; forward simulation predicts its evolution under endogenous dynamics and external interventions; and interactive response produces distinct, action3 OpenEnvision Technical Report OPENENVISION conditioned futures as visual, geometric, or task-specific outputs. This decomposition is functional rather than architectural and defines shared interface, not requirement that every system implement all three operations. Static 3D methods emphasize persistent-state inference and geometry decoding, video models primarily learn implicit transitions and observation generation, 4D methods explicitly represent time-varying structure, and embodied models connect state estimation and action prediction to decision-making. Characterizing systems by the operations they implement and the capability profiles they support provides common vocabulary for comparing them. These operations alone, however, describe what system does without determining whether it qualifies as world model. Qualification is decided not by any single operation but by the state that persists across all of them: we define generative world model as learned, historyand control-conditioned dynamical system that infers and maintains persistent environmental state, evolves that state under endogenous dynamics and external interventions, and assimilates observational feedback into coherent future trajectories. Persistence in this sense is operational rather than nominal: an intervention must leave trace in the state that constrains later predictions, and each incoming observation must in turn revise that state. Only when both hold is the world-modeling loop closed. Visual plausibility, by contrast, reflects only the observation decoder; it is neither necessary nor sufficient evidence that the underlying state persists, gap that recent physicsand world-oriented benchmarks repeatedly expose [69]. It is closure, not plausibility, that draws principled boundary between foundational generative models, which synthesize or transform observations without closing the loop, and generative world models, which couple generation to an evolving environmental state through closed-loop updates. Measuring progress from foundational generation toward world intelligence therefore calls for evidence of closure, which in turn depends on shared infrastructure for reproducible execution and comprehensive, fair evaluation. We realize this infrastructure in WorldFoundry, an open-source system for integrating, executing, and evaluating video, 3D, 4D, interactive world, and embodied-action models. WorldFoundry spans the research lifecycle, from model and benchmark discovery and runtime and asset preparation to execution orchestration, artifact management, evaluation, and interactive visualization. Modality-specific adapters preserve native execution and evaluation semantics; declarative manifests specify dependencies, assets, and interfaces; durable artifact contracts decouple execution from evaluation; and evidence-aware scorecards separate declared support, operational readiness, and validated performance. The current release integrates 270 models and over 100 benchmark and metric implementations, with every model runner validated through end-to-end execution of documented reference workflow. By combining our theory of world modeling with the proposed infrastructure, WorldFoundry transforms isolated generative demonstrations into cumulative, auditable evidence and advances the field from perceptual synthesis toward measurable world intelligence. Our key contributions can be summarized as follows: World Model Definition. We formally define world models through minimal abstraction comprising state inference, forward simulation, and interactive response. We then characterize the core capabilities of perception, modeling, manipulation, dynamics, and interaction within structured functional framework, thereby organizing and differentiating existing generative and world-modeling systems. Unified Inference and Evaluation Infrastructure. We introduce WorldFoundry, an open-source infrastructure that standardizes execution and evaluation across video, 3D, 4D, embodied-action, and interactive world systems, making inference reproducible and configurable without overriding native model semantics, and placing heterogeneous systems under common operational definition of world modeling. Validation at Scale. We integrate 270 generative models and over 100 benchmark and metric implementations. We validate every model runner through documented end-to-end reference workflow, yielding an auditable record of operational readiness under the tested configurations. 4 OpenEnvision Technical Report OPENENVISION

sections.title:
2.1 World Models and Research Infrastructure
Learned world models link environmental prediction to planning and control. World Models [1] combined
compact visual representations with recurrent dynamics and policy learning; PlaNet [2] planned through
latent dynamics, while DreamerV3 [3] learned policies from imagined trajectories. Research on video
generation, spatial reconstruction, and embodied control introduces diverse conditioning schemes, state
representations, and execution requirements. Specialized toolkits address these requirements within individual
domains: Diffusers [17] organizes generative pipelines, Nerfstudio [25] supports neural reconstruction and
rendering, LeRobot [18] and StarVLA [19] support policy development and deployment, and Isaac Lab [26]
provides simulation and learning workflows. World-model platforms cover broader development lifecycles.
Cosmos [11, 12] combines data preparation, foundation models, and post-training, complemented by scoring
orchestration and durable result storage in Cosmos Evaluator [13]. Genie Envisioner and GE-Sim 2.0 [14, 15]
connect action-conditioned video simulation with robot-policy evaluation and learning, while minWM [16]
supports fine-tuning and distillation for controllable autoregressive generation. OpenWorldLib [5, 10] is
the most closely related infrastructure for heterogeneous integration: its pipeline, operator, representation,
reasoning, and memory modules unify video, spatial, and embodied systems through common interfaces,
supporting multi-turn execution and evaluation from saved results. Its formulation emphasizes perception,
interaction, and long-term memory. WorldFoundry couples an operational criterion grounded in persistent state,
intervention effects, and observational feedback (§3.1–3.2) with explicit execution contracts: manifests specify
runtime and asset requirements, serializable requests preserve native controls, and typed artifact references
link outputs to execution provenance. These contracts connect model invocation, artifact management, and
evaluation within a shared experimental lifecycle; general training remains future work.

sections.title: 3 Unified Definition of World Modeling
sections.content: Figure 2 World Modeling. State inference maintains persistent environment representation from observations; forward simulation predicts coherent state transitions; interactive response produces action-conditioned futures. Observation feedback updates the state for subsequent predictions. fundamental obstacle to progress in generative world modeling research is the absence of precise and shared conceptual foundation. Without an operational definition of what constitutes world model and principled criterion for distinguishing it from related systems, the field risks conflating fundamentally different modeling objectives. This section aims to address this gap. We first establish an operational definition of world modeling; we then situate the model landscape along an intelligence-oriented capability progression that traces increasingly demanding functional behaviors; finally, we formulate principled boundary between foundational generative models that synthesize observations and generative world models that simulate world. 6 OpenEnvision Technical Report OPENENVISION

sections.title:
3.1 What is World Model: An Operational Definition
Motivated by previous work on learned world models in reinforcement learning [1–3], we characterize world
modeling by three tightly coupled operations over task-relevant latent state rather than observations alone:
(i) state inference, which estimates latent environmental state from observations; (ii) forward simulation,
which predicts state evolution under autonomous dynamics, physical constraints, and external actions; and
(iii) interactive response, which adapts predicted futures coherently under alternative actions or interventions.

Newly acquired observations update the maintained state and inform further generation. The defining property is therefore the coupling of observation synthesis with persistent state, intervention-conditioned dynamics, and observational feedback. sections.title: 3.2 What World Models Can Do: Capability Progression
sections.content: Figure 3 Capability progression from generative modeling toward world modeling. Perceptual grounding provides the foundation; persistent state modeling, dynamics-aware prediction, and closed-loop interaction form the world-model spine; controllable transformation provides an orthogonal capability for manipulation. To situate existing generative systems with respect to this definition, we organize them along capability progression in which generation becomes increasingly grounded in an evolving environmental state. Perceptual Grounding constitutes the foundation: the capability to interpret, reconstruct, or synthesize observations without maintaining persistent environmental state. The World-Model Spine comprises three successive stages, each building on its predecessor: Persistent State Modeling infers and maintains structured environmental state across observations; Dynamics-Aware Prediction predicts physically and causally coherent transitions of that state under endogenous dynamics and external interventions; and Closed-Loop Interaction sustains repeated cycles of action, observation, and state update, in which each observation revises the state that conditions subsequent predictions. Controllable Transformation, the capability to modify represented entities, attributes, or configurations as specified while preserving content outside the scope of the edit, is orthogonal to the spine and can complement any of its stages; by itself, however, it entails none of the spine capabilities. Rather than assigning each system to single discrete level, the progression characterizes it by capability profile: which capabilities it exhibits and the degree to which they are integrated. Foundational Capability: Perceptual Grounding Perceptual Grounding (Perception) is the capability to interpret, reconstruct, or synthesize observable content. It captures structure at the observation level, supplying the perceptual basis for state inference without itself maintaining persistent representation of the underlying environment. 8 OpenEnvision Technical Report OPENENVISION World-Model Spine Persistent State Dynamics Prediction Interactive Feedback Spine I: Persistent State Modeling Persistent State Modeling (Modeling) is the capability to infer, maintain, and recursively update structured representation of environmental state from sequential observations. This representation tracks task-relevant entities and their identities, geometry, spatial relations, and latent attributes across viewpoint changes and occlusions under partial observability. Spine II: Dynamics-Aware Prediction Dynamics-Aware Prediction (Dynamics) is the capability to predict environmental state transitions in accordance with physical and causal regularities. It propagates the effects of endogenous processes, entity interactions, and external interventions through the evolving state, producing temporally coherent trajectories in which earlier events constrain later predictions through their persisting consequences. Spine III: Closed-Loop Interaction Closed-Loop Interaction (Interaction) is the capability to sustain recurrent cycles of action, environmental transition, observation, and state update within persistent environment. Feedback from observed action outcomes revises the maintained state, which in turn conditions subsequent predictions and actions, preserving causal continuity across successive interactions. Orthogonal Capability: Controllable Transformation Controllable Transformation (Manipulation) is the capability to modify represented content or state according to specified controls while preserving properties and structural relations outside the intended scope of the edit. As an orthogonal capability, it can complement any stage of the progression, but on its own establishes neither persistent state modeling nor coherent dynamics or closed-loop interaction. Taken together, these capabilities characterize world intelligence through their integration rather than their individual strength: observations update persistent state, state constrains predictions, and action outcomes inform subsequent inference and interaction. Current systems occupy this progression unevenly. Video generators achieve strong perceptual grounding with largely implicit state; 3D and 4D methods maintain explicit spatial structure but rarely predict its evolution under actions; interactive world models close the loop over short horizons and have begun to address longer-range memory; and embodied policies act within persistent environments under narrow task and embodiment coverage. Evaluating where system sits therefore requires evidence about the cycle itself, not only about output quality. Existing benchmarks test complementary segments of this progression: visual and physical fidelity [6, 8], camera-controlled world generation [22], interactive memory [28], and downstream embodied utility [9, 23].

sections.title:
3.3 Taxonomy: Foundational Generative Models and Generative World Models
Building on the definition and capability progression above, we draw a single boundary through contemporary
generative systems: whether a system closes the world-modeling loop. Models that primarily generate or
transform observations count as foundational generative models, even with partial, local, or implicit dynamics,
unless they maintain persistent state, support intervention-conditioned dynamics, and assimilate observational
feedback. Generative world models, by contrast, meet all three conditions: they maintain latent world states
sections.content: 9 OpenEnvision Technical Report OPENENVISION that evolve under intervention and are revised by incoming observations. Foundational Generative Models learn visual, geometric, or spatiotemporal priors for synthesis, reconstruction, and controllable manipulation, but do not integrate state, dynamics, and feedback into complete worldmodeling loop. Their defining limitation is the inability to maintain an evolving environmental state that preserves intervention effects and incorporates observational feedback into subsequent predictions. Strong individual capabilities therefore do not suffice to sustain coherent, revisable model of the world. Generative World Models, by contrast, integrate persistent state, intervention-conditioned dynamics, and observational feedback into complete world-modeling loop. Their defining property is functional coupling: intervention effects persist across state transitions, while each new observation revises the state governing subsequent predictions. Generation is thereby made accountable to an evolving environmental model, supplying functional basis for world intelligence, the capacity to anticipate the consequences of intervention and to revise those expectations through interaction.

sections.title: 4 WorldFoundry Design
sections.content: Assessing the capabilities defined above requires reproducible experiments that tie observed behavior to explicitly specified tasks and evaluation conditions. Existing implementations, however, rely on incompatible environments, input conventions, execution procedures, artifact formats, and evaluation protocols, making it difficult to tell whether observed differences arise from model capabilities or from the surrounding experimental pipelines. This fragmentation also blurs the distinctions among catalog inclusion, successful inference, partial validation, and benchmark reproduction, which are often conflated under single notion of model support. Related infrastructures address complementary aspects of this problem, including OpenWorldLib for worldmodel inference [5], Cosmos for physical-AI model development [11], and StarVLA for modular embodied-policy research [19]. Common to all of these settings is central design challenge: preserving model-specific execution semantics while making explicit what has been executed, under what conditions, and which conclusions the resulting evidence supports. We introduce WorldFoundry as open-source infrastructure organized around common lifecycle of discovery, runtime preparation, execution, inspection, and evaluation. It serves three functions. (I) It integrates declarative model and benchmark catalogs with explicit runtime, dependency, and asset management, allowing researchers to discover, configure, and execute foundational generative models for video, 3D, and 4D alongside generative world models, embodied simulators, and vision-language-action, vision-action, and world-action models, while preserving native execution semantics. (II) It decouples execution from evaluation through durable artifacts and serializable request and result contracts, so that generated videos, spatial representations, actions, trajectories, and execution traces can be inspected, reused, compared, and scored without re-instantiating the originating model or runtime; run manifests, sample results, metric summaries, reports, and scorecards record the provenance and evidential scope of each experiment. (III) It provides interactive interfaces for configuring runs, issuing control inputs, visualizing multimodal outputs, comparing results across model families, and diagnosing failures throughout generation, interaction, and evaluation.

sections.title:
4.1 System Overview
WorldFoundry is organized around a user-oriented, capability-aware research lifecycle that brings heterogeneous
visual generation and world-modeling systems into a coherent operational framework. Rather than requiring
users to navigate fragmented, model-specific inference scripts and disconnected evaluation pipelines, it
establishes shared conventions for model discovery, runtime preparation, execution, artifact inspection,
and evidence-based evaluation while preserving model-specific semantics. The framework comprises five
components (Figure 1), each described in a subsequent subsection.
(1) Surface Layer provides consistent
user-facing access through a terminal interface, command-line tools, a browser workspace, a Python API,
and programmatic interfaces. (2) Unified Inference and Interaction resolves model configurations, runtime
profiles, and required assets, and supports both stateless generation and stateful interaction through shared
request and execution pathways without altering model-native inputs, parameters, or execution semantics.
(3) Artifact and Representation Contracts specify how requests, results, generated outputs, state traces, and
execution records are materialized as durable, inspectable artifacts with explicit identity, semantics, metadata,
sections.content: 10 OpenEnvision Technical Report OPENENVISION and provenance. (4) Evaluation and Evidence applies compatible metrics and benchmark protocols to these artifacts and records per-sample results, aggregate scores, coverage, validation status, unresolved blockers, and comparison eligibility. (5) Model and Benchmark Zoo maintains manifest-driven registries of models, benchmarks, tasks, runtime profiles, assets, evaluators, readiness states, and known blockers. Across these components, persistent artifacts form the explicit boundary between execution and assessment. This separation allows computationally expensive outputs to be inspected, compared, rescored, and audited without re-executing the originating model, and keeps catalog inclusion, runnable integration, bounded validation, and complete benchmark reproduction as distinct claims rather than single notion of support.

sections.title:
4.2 Surface Layer
The Surface Layer offers multiple user-facing interfaces that share a single orchestration path, ensuring
consistent execution and evaluation across access modes. The terminal user interface (TUI) guides discovery
by querying model and benchmark catalogs, checking requirements and readiness, and resolving an executable
command before resources are allocated. The command-line interface (CLI) covers discovery, preparation,
inference, evaluation, validation, and reporting, and is designed for automated experimentation and repro-
ducible benchmarking. The browser-based Workspace supports multi-model job configuration, model-specific
input specification, runtime selection, execution monitoring, artifact inspection, and cross-run comparison,
while the single-model Studio offers tailored controls for interactive use and detailed inspection. Python and
MCP interfaces extend this functionality to external programs and agents. Every surface translates user intent
into normalized requests that are resolved against shared catalogs, runtime profiles, Pipelines, Operators,
and result contracts; this shared resolution keeps results comparable regardless of how a run is launched.

sections.title:
4.3 Unified Inference and Interaction
WorldFoundry resolves inference and interaction requests through a manifest-driven execution sequence.
Each model identifier or alias is mapped to a canonical catalog entry whose manifest specifies provenance,
supported tasks and variants, input and output modalities, required assets, runtime configuration, execution
binding, and readiness constraints. Given the requested task and variant, the resolver verifies environment
and asset compatibility and availability, reports blockers, and selects an execution backend. Once resolution
succeeds, the input is encoded as a GenerationRequest, which defines common fields for sample identity,
task context, conditioning inputs, control signals, generation parameters, and output specifications while
retaining model-specific payloads. This contract standardizes orchestration without imposing uniform input
semantics: video systems retain temporal and media-conditioning semantics; 3D and 4D systems retain
camera, coordinate-frame, geometry, and rendering semantics; embodied systems retain observation–action
schemas and simulator contracts; and interactive world models retain session state and sequential controls.
The corresponding GenerationResult records execution status, timing, errors, the resolved configuration,
and artifact references, establishing a common basis for traceability and downstream evaluation.
sections.content: 13 OpenEnvision Technical Report OPENENVISION Given resolved GenerationRequest, the WorldModelRunner coordinates execution through two complementary abstractions: an Operator and Pipeline. The Operator handles task-specific adaptation, including input validation, preprocessing, translation into model-native arguments, postprocessing, and conversion of native outputs into framework-compatible artifacts. The Pipeline manages the model lifecycle and inference runtime, including model construction, checkpoint loading, device placement, runtime configuration, distributed execution, and invocation of native inference procedures. This division separates model adaptation from runtime management while accommodating domain-specific dependencies and simulator integration. Interactive systems may retain resident Pipeline and session state, allowing successive actions or conditions to update the environment without repeated checkpoint loading or runtime initialization. Artifact references and execution metadata populate the GenerationResult; benchmark runners subsequently consume the materialized outputs and provenance records, decoupling evaluation from model loading and inference.

sections.title:
4.4 Artifact and Representation Contracts
WorldFoundry defines a two-level contract system that separates sample-level execution from run-level
organization. A GenerationRequest represents a single execution unit: inputs contains text, source media,
or task-specific observations; controls specifies action sequences, camera trajectories, or other control signals;
generation_kwargs retains model-native parameters such as random seeds and frame rates; and output_-
schema declares expected artifact types and structural requirements. The corresponding GenerationResult
records stable sample and model identifiers, execution status, errors, timing, resolved metadata, and output
references. Each materialized output is described by an ArtifactRef, which identifies externally stored
content by its semantic role and URI, with optional MIME type, media properties, file size, and content
hash. Being JSON-serializable, these contracts persist, transfer, and can be inspected across process and
environment boundaries independently of the originating model implementation.
sections.content: The contracts standardize artifact identification, provenance, references, and run organization while preserving native encodings and modality-specific semantics across media, geometry, dynamic 4D representations, actions, and state traces. At the run level, execution_plan.json specifies intended stages and sample identifiers; requests.jsonl and results.jsonl retain corresponding requests and outcomes; sample_ledger.jsonl tracks per-stage status and failures; artifacts.jsonl indexes materialized outputs; and run_manifest.json records the resolved run identity, configuration, runtime context, and output locations. Failed requests remain explicit in result and ledger records, preserving traceability and coverage accounting. This persistent record structure decouples artifact inspection and evaluation from model execution, enabling outputs to be transferred, rescored, compared, and audited without reloading the originating model. It also distinguishes structural conformance, artifact availability, qualitative validity, and benchmark eligibility as separate claims requiring appropriate evidence.

sections.title:
4.5 Evaluation and Evidence
WorldFoundry treats evaluation as an artifact-centered process, allowing scoring to proceed independently of
the originating model runtime once the required outputs are materialized. The evaluation pipeline resolves the
model, benchmark, metrics, data source, runtime profile, and output directory, and maps task or dataset entries
to GenerationRequest records with stable sample identifiers, split assignments, and input keys. It supports
scoring existing GenerationResult records, generating outputs for registered metrics, executing a complete
model–benchmark evaluation, and applying benchmark-specific evaluators to existing artifact directories.
Metrics and benchmarks carry distinct responsibilities: metrics compute per-sample measurements and
aggregate statistics from compatible artifacts, spanning semantic alignment, quality, distributional similarity,
perceptual comparison, and editing or layout assessment, whereas benchmarks additionally prescribe data,
sample coverage, preprocessing, artifact layout, evaluator assets, judge configuration, and aggregation rules,
with benchmark runners implementing protocol-specific logic and normalizing external evaluator outputs into
a shared result structure. Dependencies and evaluator checkpoints are declared explicitly, and unavailable
resources yield explicit skipped or failed states rather than undeclared substitutions.
sections.content: The evidence layer records evaluation outcomes and the conditions under which they support scientific comparisons. Each evaluation preserves its execution plan, configuration, environment and code revision, request and result records, sample coverage, stage-level errors, metric outputs, artifact references, and unresolved 14 OpenEnvision Technical Report OPENENVISION blockers. Per-sample measurements are stored in metrics/per_sample.jsonl, aggregate values and failed or skipped sample identifiers in metrics/summary.json, and run metadata and reproducibility fingerprint in run_manifest.json. These records inform scorecard.json, the authoritative machine-readable record of score validity, provenance, protocol fidelity, coverage, and comparison eligibility. Derived summary.json and report.md files provide concise machine-readable and human-readable views consistent with the scorecard. Evidence is classified as diagnostic, benchmark-comparable, or an exact benchmark reproduction according to fidelity to the prescribed generation settings, data, evaluator, runtime, and reference configuration. Importing official results validates result normalization, while bounded evaluator run demonstrates integration operability; neither alone establishes complete benchmark reproduction. Leaderboard eligibility further requires prescribed data and coverage, verified evaluator, compatible runtime evidence, successful metric computation, and no disqualifying blockers. These distinctions constrain reported claims to the available evidence, preventing successful execution or score production from being mistaken for benchmark validity.

sections.title:
4.6 Model and Benchmark Zoo
The Model Zoo is a manifest-driven registry that links model discovery to explicit, auditable integration states.
Entries fall into five operational categories: video models for conditional generation, editing, animation, and
audiovisual synthesis; generative world models for interactive environments, navigation, and simulation; 3D and
4D models for reconstruction, depth estimation, and static or dynamic scene representations; vision-language-
action, vision-action, and world-action models for embodied prediction and control; and provider-hosted
models accessed remotely. These categories reflect integration requirements rather than mutually exclusive
capabilities. Each entry has a stable identifier and optional aliases, with a manifest documenting official
sources, licensing and access conditions, tasks and variants, checkpoint references, input and artifact contracts,
runtime bindings, hardware requirements, and blockers. Linked records specify runtime contracts, execution
backends, and readiness; environment requirements, including Python and CUDA versions, package constraints,
validation imports, and environment isolation; and the concrete Pipeline implementation. Evidence records
distinguish source-reported results from those obtained through WorldFoundry, while checkpoints, credentials,
and other protected or machine-dependent assets remain outside the repository and are resolved through
explicit references. Catalog inclusion therefore establishes discoverability, not executable support: source
availability, implementation status, asset readiness, runtime validation, and execution evidence are tracked
independently, and entries remain planned or blocked until the relevant requirements are met.
sections.content: The Benchmark Zoo is parallel registry that links benchmark discovery to task construction, evaluator execution, result normalization, and evidence reporting, covering video quality, semantic alignment, physical and dynamical consistency, camera and spatial behavior, 3D and 4D understanding, interactive world modeling, safety, memory, and embodied control. Each entry has stable identifier and optional aliases and documentation of target domains, official sources, datasets and splits, task definitions, sample coverage, artifact requirements, metrics, evaluator assets, judge requirements, result formats, runtime profiles, and blockers. Task manifests define how dataset records or prompts become reproducible sample requests, while benchmark manifests specify the evaluation protocol and the supported execution path that most closely follows it. This path may use an in-framework evaluator, an external official runtime, an official-result importer, hosted judge, or simulator interface. Integration verification is recorded separately from eligibility for benchmark comparison: importing schema-conformant official result verifies parsing and normalization, whereas reproducing an official evaluation also requires the prescribed data, artifact coverage, dependencies, assets, credentials, runtime conditions, and protocol settings. Models and benchmarks are paired only when their declared task semantics and artifact requirements are compatible. sections.title: 5 Empirical Validation and Analysis
sections.content: We evaluate WorldFoundry using representative models for video generation, interactive world modeling, 3D and 4D generation, and embodied action prediction and control. The evaluation first verifies whether the framework preserves native input and output semantics and produces results consistent with native implementations under matched conditions. It then examines whether equivalent requests issued through the CLI, Python API, and web interface yield consistent configurations and execution behavior. Latency and GPU memory overhead are profiled last, together with the effort required to integrate new model. 16 OpenEnvision Technical Report OPENENVISION

sections.title:
5.2.1 Video Generation.
For video generation, we consider text-to-video synthesis, image-to-video synthesis, and video-to-video editing.
These tasks assess whether a model can generate plausible visual dynamics, preserve subject identity and
scene structure over time, and satisfy task-specific conditions, capabilities central to modeling how the visual
world evolves. Successful generation therefore requires both fidelity to the supplied conditions and coherent
temporal progression in appearance, spatial relationships, and motion. Depending on the task, inputs consist
of a textual description alone or of visual conditions, such as reference images or source videos, paired
with instructions specifying the desired content, motion, or transformation; additional reference modalities
and structural constraints are supplied where the model supports them. Representative systems include
CogVideoX [31], Vchitect-2.0 [32], HunyuanVideo 1.5 [33], LTX-2.5 [34], Wan2.1 [35], Wan2.1 VACE [36],
Wan2.2 [37], LingBot-Video [38], and MiniMax H3 [39], which span diverse conditioning mechanisms and
generation pipelines. WorldFoundry preserves each system’s native input processing and inference settings, so
that results reflect its intended operation. Figure 7 shows representative text-to-video results from LTX-2.5,
Wan2.2, and MiniMax H3, covering both camera motion through largely static scenes and object-centric
dynamics such as running animals and a hovering bird.
sections.content: Qualitative analysis highlights distinct strengths across generation tasks. In text-conditioned synthesis, CogVideoX and Vchitect-2.0 capture scene composition and broad motion patterns, but complex motion and multi-object interactions expose inconsistencies in identity, fine detail, and spatial relationships. FLAG3D++ [40] provides detailed and professional language instructions to describe how to perform specific activity, as well as the corresponding accurate and dense 3D human pose captured from an advanced MoCap system to handle complex activities and large movements. HunyuanVideo 1.5 and Wan2.1 produce coherent short sequences, particularly with image conditioning, although appearance preservation does not consistently translate into plausible motion under occlusion or substantial deformation. Published results for Wan2.2 [37] report improvements in motion generation and aesthetic control over Wan2.1, extending the range of visually convincing sequences. LingBot-Video provides complementary advance: its reported post-training comparisons [38] show reduced object deformation, interpenetration, and premature object release, indicating gains in physical interaction beyond perceptual quality alone. MiniMax H3 broadens reference-based generation and editing, with official demonstrations combining appearance, motion, and audio cues from different sources [39]; these examples demonstrate compositional flexibility but do not establish reliable physical dynamics. Together, these observations suggest that progress unfolds along several distinct dimensions: visual refinement, preservation of conditioning information, and consistency of the depicted events. sequence may remain visually smooth and recognizable while violating contact relations or failing to complete the requested transformation, which makes event-level consistency necessary complement to frame-level quality in video-generation analysis. 17 OpenEnvision Technical Report OPENENVISION Figure 7 Demonstration of inference results from representative video generation models.

sections.title:
5.2.2 Interactive World Model.
For interactive world modeling, we consider navigation, camera-controlled exploration, and action- or
instruction-driven interaction within generated environments. These tasks assess whether a model can
maintain a coherent environment as actions unfold, retain information beyond the immediate visual context,
and carry the consequences of earlier interactions into subsequent predictions. Unlike offline video synthe-
sis, the model produces an evolving observation stream conditioned on successive interventions, allowing
later actions to respond to previously generated observations. Inputs comprise an initial image or image
sequence, the available interaction history, and model-supported controls, including directional movement,
camera rotation, discrete game actions, and textual instructions. Successful generation therefore requires
both immediate responsiveness to controls and persistent consistency in scene geometry, object identity,
and interaction outcomes, including when previously observed regions are revisited. Representative systems
include the Matrix-Game series up to the recent 3.5 release [41], LingBot-World 1.0 and 2.0 [42, 43], Hunyuan
GameCraft and GameCraft-2 [44, 45], YUME-1.5 [46], HY-WorldPlay [47], SCOPE [48], SANA-WM [49],
and Echo-WM [50]. WorldFoundry preserves each system’s native action vocabulary, history-conditioning
mechanism, and generation schedule, and records controls, observations, and runtime configurations to support
reproducible trajectory-level analysis. Figure 8 shows 30-second rollouts from five representative systems
driven by directional movement and mouse-based camera control across diverse scenes.
sections.content: Qualitative comparison highlights progress along two complementary dimensions: scene persistence and 18 OpenEnvision Technical Report OPENENVISION interaction expressiveness. Matrix-Game 2.0 [51] enables responsive navigation but exhibits appearance drift over extended rollouts, whereas LingBot-World 1.0, Hunyuan GameCraft, YUME-1.5, and HY-WorldPlay produce visually coherent navigation sequences in the examined cases. Recent memory-augmented systems address consistency beyond the immediate context: Matrix-Game 3.0 [52] introduces long-horizon memory, while published results for Matrix-Game 3.5 [41] and ReWorld [53] demonstrate scene recall through geometryaware retrieval and pose-indexed landmarks, respectively. These advances make revisitation more informative than uninterrupted forward motion for assessing whether model retains previously observed content. In parallel, LingBot-World 2.0 [43] and Hunyuan-GameCraft-2 [45] broaden interaction to diverse actions and instruction-driven events, while SCOPE [48] demonstrates localized firing and reloading responses alongside continuous movement and camera control. However, scene recall and action responsiveness are distinct from persistent interaction outcomes: recovering familiar view does not establish that an opened door remains open or that displaced object retains its new position after leaving the field of view. The resulting evaluation priority is therefore to distinguish memory of scene appearance from memory of changes caused by actions. Reliable interactive world modeling requires both: stable recovery of unchanged content and consistent propagation of action-dependent state changes across subsequent observations. Figure 8 Demonstration of inference results from representative world models. 5.2.3 3D & 4D Generation. For 3D and 4D generation, we consider static scene reconstruction, scene synthesis, and dynamic scene modeling. These tasks assess whether model can recover or generate spatial structure, maintain consistency across viewpoints, and represent changes over time. Successful reconstruction requires geometry and camera estimates consistent with the observed views, while conditional synthesis requires spatially coherent content that follows the supplied visual or textual conditions. Dynamic scene modeling additionally requires distinguishing camera motion from scene motion and preserving temporal correspondence through deformation, occlusion, and reappearance. Depending on the task, inputs comprise single images, multi-view observations, video sequences, or textual descriptions, and outputs include point maps, camera parameters, point clouds, meshes, Gaussian representations, and time-dependent geometry. Representative systems include DUSt3R [54], 19 OpenEnvision Technical Report OPENENVISION CUT3R [55], VGGT [56], VGGT-Omega [57], Splatt3R [58], and FlashWorld [59] for spatial reconstruction or synthesis, alongside MonST3R [60], NeoVerse [61], and Lyra [62] for complementary video-based and spatiotemporal workflows. Evaluation criteria include camera consistency, reconstruction completeness, novel-view quality, inference efficiency, and, where reference geometry is available, geometric accuracy, with additional attention to temporal stability in dynamic scenes. WorldFoundry preserves each methods native inputs and representations, organizes comparisons within compatible task families, and records configurations, rendered views, and exported artifacts for reproducible spatial and temporal analysis. Figure 9 compares VGGT, VGGT-Omega, DUSt3R, and CUT3R on the same indoor scene, rendering each reconstruction from common sequence of viewpoints. Qualitative analysis highlights distinction between reconstructing observed structure and generating plausible spatial completion. DUSt3R recovers geometry through pairwise point-map prediction, while VGGT jointly estimates camera parameters, depth, point maps, and point tracks from multiple views; VGGT-Omega further develops this feed-forward reconstruction paradigm. Splatt3R complements geometric reconstruction with Gaussian appearance attributes for novel-view rendering, although convincing rendered views do not establish accurate geometry in sparsely observed or occluded regions. FlashWorld enables efficient scene synthesis through direct Gaussian generation, while Lyra transfers video-generation priors into feed-forward 3D and 4D reconstruction, illustrating how learned priors can supply plausible content beyond the available observations. In dynamic scenes, MonST3R accommodates scene motion when estimating geometry and cameras, and NeoVerse extends monocular reconstruction to time-varying scenes and novel camera trajectories. The central ambiguity is whether image changes arise from camera motion, object motion, or newly visible surfaces: temporal smoothness alone cannot establish correct geometric correspondence. For extended exploration, Lyra 2.0 [63] reports improved consistency through geometry-guided retrieval and training that mitigates accumulated generation drift. Together, these developments motivate distinguishing three properties: agreement with observed evidence, cross-view consistency of inferred content, and temporal persistence of scene structure. representation can be visually convincing and internally consistent while remaining inaccurate in unobserved regions; reconstructing dynamic sequence likewise does not establish the ability to predict its evolution under alternative actions. sections.title:
5.2.4 Embodied Action Generation.
For embodied action generation, we consider visual policy learning, language-conditioned manipulation, and
control informed by predicted environmental dynamics. These tasks assess whether a model can translate
observations and task specifications into executable actions, coordinate perception with control, and adapt to
feedback during execution. Inputs comprise visual observations and proprioceptive states, supplemented by
natural-language instructions or predicted future observations where supported. Outputs comprise discrete
actions, continuous control commands, or action sequences expressed in the target embodiment’s native
action space. The integrated systems follow three complementary paradigms: Vision-Action (VA) policies,
which generate actions from visual and robot-state observations; Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models,
which additionally incorporate linguistic instructions; and World-Action Models (WAMs), which couple action
generation with predictions of environmental evolution. Representative integrations include Action Chunking
Transformer [64], OpenVLA [65], RoboFlamingo [66], MolmoAct2 [67], GigaBrain-0 [68], Being-H0.5 [69],
StarVLA [19], LingBot-VLA 1.0 and 2.0 [70, 71], and LingBot-VA 1.0 and 2.0 [72, 73]. Evaluation combines
offline action prediction with closed-loop execution in compatible manipulation environments, including
LIBERO and RoboTwin [74, 75]; criteria include task completion, instruction adherence, control accuracy,
trajectory smoothness, execution latency, and recovery from intermediate errors. WorldFoundry preserves
each system’s observation history, camera configuration, action coordinates, normalization statistics, control
frequency, and action-chunk horizon, with comparisons restricted to compatible embodiments and task
protocols. Figure 10 shows closed-loop LIBERO-10 episodes of OpenVLA executed through WorldFoundry:
the policy completes a single-object pick-and-place task but reaches the step limit on two multi-stage tasks,
illustrating why closed-loop completion, rather than offline action accuracy, is the relevant measure.
sections.content: Published empirical findings indicate that semantic grounding, embodiment transfer, and predictive control contribute to embodied competence through distinct mechanisms. SuperMimic [76] demonstrates that shared differentiable world model can efficiently scale humanoid whole-body control through short imagined rollouts and analytic policy gradients, substantially reducing the computational cost of policy learning. OpenVLA [65] and RoboFlamingo [66] demonstrate that pretrained vision-language representations can support languageconditioned manipulation, although transfer remains dependent on the target embodiment and adaptation data. MolmoAct2 [67] combines embodied reasoning with dedicated action expert, exposing trade-off between additional spatial reasoning and control latency. GigaBrain-0 [68] improves generalization through world-model-generated training data, whereas Being-H0.5 [69] aligns human and robot motion within shared action representation. StarVLA [19] provides complementary policy variants for examining how action decoding and training choices affect execution, rather than defining single control mechanism. LingBot-VLA 1.0 [70] demonstrates effective adaptation across robot platforms, while LingBot-VLA 2.0 [71] extends this approach to whole-body control and incorporates future semantic and geometric prediction as auxiliary supervision. LingBot-VA 1.0 [72] instead couples video and action prediction within causal sequence model; LingBot-VA 2.0 [73] further introduces action-aligned visual representations and asynchronous inference that incorporates the latest observations during execution. These distinctions suggest that the value of world modeling depends on where prediction enters the control pipeline: as training-data augmentation, representation supervision, or an online component of action generation. In particular, plausible future observations are useful only insofar as they support executable actions and timely correction when reality departs from prediction. The decisive evidence is therefore improved closed-loop completion and recovery under comparable data, embodiment, and latency constraints, rather than predictive visual quality or offline action accuracy alone. 21 OpenEnvision Technical Report OPENENVISION Figure 10 Representative closed-loop embodied results. OpenVLA executed through WorldFoundry on LIBERO10, with one recorded episode per task. The policy completes task (a) within 179 steps, whereas tasks (b) and (c) reach the 520-step limit before completion.

sections.title: 6 Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: Although WorldFoundry provides unified operational foundation for diverse generative world-modeling systems, its broad coverage encompasses different levels of execution maturity. Catalog inclusion, runnable integration, local asset readiness, official runtime validation, and benchmark eligibility remain distinct states, reflecting the external checkpoints, licensed datasets, hosted services, simulator assets, and dedicated environments required by individual models and benchmarks. Differences in architecture and hardware requirements also prevent single optimization strategy from benefiting every video, spatial, interactive, and embodied model equally. In addition, the present framework focuses on inference, interaction, artifact management, and evaluation. general training infrastructure remains direction for future development, and upstream training code is intentionally separated from current runtime packages. This scope provides 22 OpenEnvision Technical Report OPENENVISION consistent and auditable foundation for experimentation, while leaving opportunities to extend lifecycle reproducibility as public datasets and reproducible training recipes become available across domains. The inference core already exposes broad set of optimization mechanisms: configurable attention backends, including FlashAttention 2 [77] and 3 [78], SageAttention [79], xFormers, and SDPA; Triton kernel registration; compilation and inference caching; NVFP4 quantization where supported; hardware-aware GPU selection; and multi-GPU context and sequence parallelism. Their effects, however, have not yet been characterized systematically across model families, and validation has primarily used A100 and H100 GPUs; limited access to B200and B300-class systems constrains assessment on newer accelerators. Future work will combine broader hardware validation with runtime profiling, automatic backend selection, improved compilation and cache reuse, fidelity-aware quantization, and more efficient memory management and distributed execution. We will also integrate dedicated serving engines through modular backend adapters and runtime profiles that preserve native input semantics, artifact contracts, and evaluation protocols. Improvements will be assessed by end-to-end latency, throughput, memory use, scaling efficiency, and reproducibility, since kernel-level acceleration alone does not establish application-level gains. An optimization will be adopted only if its outputs remain within declared fidelity tolerance of the unoptimized route. Beyond inference optimization, we plan to extend WorldFoundry to support data preparation and training. Initial development will focus on representative baselines and public datasets, reflecting the uneven availability of reproducible training recipes across domains. The extension will support versioned dataset manifests, distributed training, fine-tuning and post-training, checkpoint lineage, experiment recovery, and direct checkpoint registration in the Model Zoo. Existing contracts will link data and optimization configurations to checkpoints, inference artifacts, and benchmark results. Since reproducible training alone does not guarantee consistent deployment behavior, we will explicitly align preprocessing, conditioning, normalization, coordinate conventions, and checkpoint interpretation across training and inference. Reusable configurations, guided setup, and actionable diagnostics will ease adoption while retaining domain-specific controls. Training, execution, and evaluation will remain distinct responsibilities within an auditable research lifecycle, preserving architectural flexibility and traceability from data preparation to reported results.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduce WorldFoundry as open-source infrastructure built on an operational definition of generative world models as systems with persistent state, intervention-conditioned dynamics, and observational feedback. This definition shifts the criterion for world modeling from the quality of individual outputs to the behavior of the loop that produces them: generated observation counts as evidence of world model only insofar as it is constrained by state that past interventions have altered and that new observations can revise. WorldFoundry relies on this view across video, 3D and 4D, interactive world, and embodied action systems, cataloging 270 model entries, 74 benchmarks, and 62 metrics under shared contracts that preserve native semantics. By recording catalog inclusion, executability, and validated performance as distinct claims, it keeps every reported result traceable to the artifacts and conditions that support it. Our cross-family analysis indicates that visual fidelity, scene consistency, and action responsiveness, although complementary, cannot by themselves certify world modeling; what current evaluations seldom measure is whether intervention effects persist and whether incoming observations correct the state. Future work will develop evaluations that directly probe intervention persistence and feedback assimilation, alongside broader inference optimization, hardware validation, and reproducible training with explicit traininginference consistency. By connecting capability definitions, executable workflows, and traceable evidence, WorldFoundry provides shared foundation for measuring progress toward world intelligence. 23 OpenEnvision Technical Report OPENENVISION

sections.content: Table 11 lists all 62 canonical entries in the WorldFoundry metric registry. The table is compiled from the metric documentation together with the registry and its module declarations, and therefore includes entries absent from the documentation summary, such as laion_aesthetic. Metrics are grouped by use into multimodal/quality scorers (10), image/feature distribution metrics (26), video distribution metrics (3), perceptual/layout metrics (11), editing metrics (7), and existing-result utilities (5). Aliases and variants map to their canonical entries and are not counted separately. The registry specifies scoring implementations; benchmark scorecard dimensions and official evaluator outputs are defined by their respective benchmark protocols. and denote the preferred direction declared for each assessment; denotes result utility with no universal quality ordering. Numeric-field direction follows the underlying reported score. Metric IDs link to their sources or implementations. Learned metrics require their declared pretrained backbones, FVD uses I3D weights, JEDi uses compatible video-encoder/probe weights, and natural_score requires an API judge. Precomputed-feature and layout routines instead consume the specified embeddings, probabilities, masks, or boxes. Support for registry entry does not by itself establish equivalence to every published evaluator configuration. Table 11 Complete supported metric catalog.
